issues.legal_issue: An appellate court should not reverse an acquittal where the evidence permits two reasonable views and the acquittal is not manifestly illegal, perverse, or a cause of miscarriage of justice.
material_facts: The trial court acquitted the accused after finding inconsistencies in the accounts of his alleged role and evidence supporting his absence from the scene.
The High Court reversed the acquittal and convicted him.

The Supreme Court found that the trial court’s view favouring the accused was reasonably available and that its judgment was not manifestly illegal, perverse, or productive of a miscarriage of justice.
issues.conclusion: The High Court should not have interfered with the acquittal; the conviction entered on reversal of that acquittal was set aside.
issues.legal_principle: The presumption of innocence is strengthened by an acquittal, and where two views are possible on the evidence, the view favourable to the accused should be adopted. An appellate court may interfere with an acquittal only for compelling and substantial reasons, such as when the judgment is clearly unreasonable or ignores admissible evidence. The Court relied on Narendra Singh v. State of M.P., State of Rajasthan v. Raja Ram, Dhanna v. State of M.P., Mahabir Singh v. State of Haryana, Shailendra Pratap v. State of U.P., Bhagwan Singh v. State of M.P., and Bindeshwari Prasad Singh v. State of Bihar.

rule.if: appeal_from_acquittal and trial_court_acquitted_on_reasonable_doubt and evidence_supports_two_views and not acquittal_manifestly_perverse

predicates.appeal_from_acquittal: The proceeding is an appeal seeking to reverse an acquittal.
predicates.trial_court_acquitted_on_reasonable_doub: The trial court acquitted the accused after finding a reasonable doubt in the prosecution evidence.
predicates.evidence_supports_two_views: The evidence permits both a view supporting guilt and a reasonable view supporting innocence.
predicates.acquittal_manifestly_perverse: The acquittal is manifestly perverse or clearly unreasonable.

issues.definition: When an appeal challenges an acquittal, the trial court found reasonable doubt, the evidence permits two views, and the acquittal is not manifestly perverse, the acquittal should not be reversed.

issues.legal_issue: A witness’s interest in the case does not by itself make the witness’s testimony unreliable or require the court to reject it.
material_facts: Two prosecution witnesses challenged on the ground of interest were the deceased children’s mother and the injured man’s wife.
The prosecution relied on their accounts of the incident, and the defence argued that their relationship to the deceased made their testimony unworthy of consideration.
issues.conclusion: The argument that the testimony should not be considered because the witnesses were interested had no merit; such testimony can carry substantial importance and weight.
issues.legal_principle: Interested witnesses’ testimony is not automatically disqualified, and a witness’s interest alone does not establish a willingness to spare the real culprit and frame an innocent person. The Court relied on Mohd. Ishaque v. State of West Bengal.

predicates.criminal_case: The testimony is being assessed in a criminal case.
predicates.witness_is_interested: The witness has a personal or relational interest in the case.

issues.definition: In a criminal case, testimony from an interested witness is not rejected solely because the witness is interested.

issues.legal_issue: A claim of juvenility may be raised before any court at any stage, and a person shown by the prescribed procedure to have been below the age of eighteen at the time of the offence is a juvenile.
material_facts: The accused raised a claim of juvenility before the Supreme Court.
A school certificate recorded a birth date that made him below eighteen at the time of the offence.
His age was determined in accordance with the procedure in Rule 12 of the Juvenile Justice Model Rules, 2007, and the Court found no doubt about that determination.
issues.conclusion: The juvenility claim was properly raised and established, and the accused was a juvenile at the time of the offence.
issues.legal_principle: Under Sections 2(k) and 7A of the Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act, 2000, a juvenility claim may be raised before any court at any stage. The age determination must follow Rule 12 of the Juvenile Justice Model Rules, 2007.

rule.if: criminal_proceeding and juvenility_claim_raised and age_below_eighteen_at_offence and age_established_by_required_procedure

predicates.criminal_proceeding: The matter is a criminal proceeding concerning an alleged offence.
predicates.juvenility_claim_raised: The accused raises a claim that the accused was a juvenile when the offence occurred.
predicates.age_below_eighteen_at_offence: The accused was below eighteen years of age when the offence occurred.
predicates.age_established_by_required_procedure: The accused’s age is established using the prescribed age-determination procedure.

issues.definition: In a criminal proceeding, when a juvenility claim is raised and the prescribed procedure establishes that the accused was below eighteen at the time of the offence, the accused was a juvenile at that time.

issues.legal_issue: A juvenile who has already undergone detention exceeding the maximum period available under the juvenile justice regime must be released, even if the conviction is assumed to stand.
material_facts: The accused was below eighteen years of age when the offence occurred.
He had undergone about eight years in jail, exceeding the maximum three-year period prescribed for a juvenile under the applicable regime.

The Court set aside the conviction on the other grounds discussed, and additionally held that even if the conviction were upheld, he had undergone more than the maximum permissible period and was entitled to release.
issues.conclusion: The accused was entitled to release; the Court allowed the appeal, set aside the High Court’s decision, and discharged his bail bonds after his release on bail.
issues.legal_principle: Section 15 of the Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act, 2000, limits the period for which a juvenile may be kept in a special home. Rule 98 of the Juvenile Justice Model Rules, 2007, was applied with that provision. The Court relied on Ajay Kumar v. State of M.P., Hakim v. State, and Lakhan Lal v. State of Bihar.

predicates.juvenile_sentencing_case: The proceeding concerns the sentence or detention of a person who was a juvenile when the offence occurred.
predicates.juvenile_at_offence: The person was a juvenile when the offence occurred.
predicates.detention_exceeds_maximum_juvenile_perio: The person has already been detained for longer than the maximum period permitted for a juvenile.

issues.definition: In a juvenile sentencing case, if the person was a juvenile at the time of the offence and has been detained beyond the maximum permitted period, the person must be released.
